A ball in a socket that lets a suspension or steering part swivel. A worn one knocks, and if it fails the wheel can collapse.
A belt-driven air pump that forces extra air into the engine. XKR cars have one.
A bolt that undoes clockwise, the opposite way to a normal bolt.
A bolt with no head, fixed into a part so that a nut can go on the free end.
A branched pipe that carries air into the engine, or exhaust gas out of it.
A chain inside the engine that keeps the valves in step with the pistons. If it slips, the engine can be badly damaged.
A face where two parts meet. It must be clean and flat so the parts sit true.
A flat rim with bolt holes, where two pipes or parts join.
A flat seal between two metal faces, so that oil, water or gas cannot leak out.
A grooved wheel that a belt runs round.
A hand tool with a shaped end that grips a nut or bolt head.
A handheld tester that measures volts, amps and resistance.
A metal bar that links the left and right suspension to keep the car level in corners.
A metal cup that fits over a nut or bolt head and turns on a handle.
A nut or bolt with a grip built in, so that it will not shake loose. The grip wears out, so it can only be reused so many times.
A part that keeps a chain or belt tight by pushing on it, with a spring or with oil pressure.
A rubber joint in the propshaft that takes out vibration.
A rubber ring that seals a joint. Fit a new one whenever the joint is opened.
A rubber sleeve in a suspension joint. It lets the joint move without metal touching metal.
A separate frame bolted under the car. It carries the suspension and sometimes the engine.
A short code, such as P0340, that the car's computer stores when it sees a problem. A code reader shows it.
A small electric switch. A weak current uses it to turn on a stronger one.
A small pipe that lets fumes out of the engine and back into the air intake.
A small valve on a brake caliper. You open it to let out air and old fluid.
A small valve that sprays fuel into the engine.
A smooth pin that the brake caliper slides on, so that the pads wear evenly.
A springy metal ring that sits in a groove to hold a part in place.
A springy wire clip shaped like a letter R. It stops a pin sliding out.
A steel beam that runs across the body of the car. It is stronger than the panels around it.
A strengthened place under the car where a jack or axle stand can safely push. Pushing anywhere else can bend the car or let it fall.
A strong metal stand that holds the car once it has been jacked up. Never go under a car held only by a jack.
A thin metal spacer used to set a gap or an angle exactly.
A thin metal spring clip on a brake caliper. It holds the pads and caliper still, so they do not rattle.
A tool that lifts the car. A trolley jack rolls on small wheels and lifts as you pump its handle. It lifts, but it does not hold the car safely.
A triangular suspension arm that joins the wheel to the car.
A turning shaft whose lobes open and close the engine's valves.
A valve that stays shut until the engine is warm, then lets coolant through to the radiator.
A warning and a safe mode: the car limits its power to protect itself until the fault is fixed.
A wedge pushed against a tyre so that the car cannot roll.
A wheel that spins freely to guide a belt.
A wrench you set to a figure. It clicks or shows you when the bolt has reached the right tightness.

The big aluminium beam under the front of the car that carries the suspension and steering. It is not a jacking point.
The bolt you undo to let old oil or coolant out.
The bracket bolted to the car that the brake caliper sits on. The pads and caliper slide on it.
The centre that the wheel bolts to. It spins on the wheel bearing.
The clamp over the brake disc. It squeezes the pads against the disc to slow the car.
The engine control module: the computer that runs the engine.
The gears at the back that send power to both rear wheels and let them turn at different speeds.
The generator, driven by a belt, that charges the battery while the engine runs.
The heavy part that holds the wheel bearing and hub. The suspension arms bolt to it.
The liquid that carries the push of your foot from the pedal to the brakes. It strips paint and soaks up water over time.
The long shaft that carries power from the gearbox to the back of the car.
The mass air flow sensor. It measures the air going into the engine.
The metal plate that turns with the wheel. The pads grip it to stop the car.
The mix of water and antifreeze that carries heat away from the engine.
The negative side of the electrics, joined to the metal of the car. It is also called the earth.
The pan at the bottom of the engine that holds the oil.
The part of the exhaust that cleans the gases before they leave the car.
The plastic bottle where you check and top up the coolant. It is under pressure when hot.
The round unit behind the brake pedal. It uses engine vacuum to make the pedal easier to press.
The thin metal rod you pull out to check a fluid level.
The toothed bar that moves the front wheels when you turn the steering wheel.
The top part of the engine, which holds the valves and spark plugs.
The valve that lets air into the engine. The accelerator pedal controls it.

To let trapped air out of a system full of liquid. Air in the brakes makes the pedal soft. Air in the cooling system can overheat the engine.
